items.title: Paul Barnes Interview, 1971-03-13
items.q: We had Louis Armstrong playing with us. He's sick now, he hardly playing anymore.

ctx.x: Yeah, that's right. The oldest one that could outblow Rene or anybody else was Louis Armstrong.

items.title: Paul Barnes Interview, 1971-03-13
items.q: Johnny Sincere, famous banjo, that was Louis Hot Five, you know.

ctx.x: Already did? Yeah. I don't remember. That's fascinating. I was just curious because you have traveled with bands both in the south and in the north and out west.

Well through my life I can see I had an opportunity to play with almost all the great musicians. We were playing together in Louis Russell's band. We had Johnny Hodges, old saxophone with us you know. And I played four years at Disneyland. And we had Johnny Sincere, he's passed. We had the great Monet Moore singing, she's passed. And then we had Louis Armstrong playing with us. He's sick now, he hardly playing anymore. And Johnny Sincere, famous banjo, that was Louis Hot Five, you know. Oh yeah. Johnny Sincere,…
Well something I wanted to ask you, you know, you played so much saxophone with all the big bands, why did you take that clarinet again?

items.title: Paul Barnes Interview, 1969-06-16
items.q: But if you would hear Louis Armstrong's old record, just like listening to Buddy Petit.

ctx.x: What bands did you hear Sidney work with? I mean, who was he playing with at this time, Sidney Bechet?

At the time before Sidney left, he was playing with a band, they called himself, the Young Olympia band. And that was with Siren Moreira, and Buddy P.T. Sometimes Buddy would send Louis Armstrong into his place, and John Marrero. They had a wonderful band. Yeah.

Did the, I mean music, when you were coming out, was it the same sort of thing as now? I mean the trumpet would just play a couple of choruses in the lead, and then they'd take solos? No, no, they didn't do that.
